doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Berklee and Joe Viola's teaching of improvisation
summary: A private student of Viola, who gave tools rather than teaching improvisation.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: What was your experience at Berklee like?

Well I was a private student of Joe’s. Joe Viola’s. I was just a private student. I never studied there. But I used to sit in the hall and listen to all the students there talk about whatever. And Joe occasionally used to sneak me into an ensemble or something like that, to give me a little experience or a sax quartet or a sax section or something. But by and large my association was with Joe Viola. He was the head of the woodwind department there and my goodness I studied with him for a long, long time. A long apprenticeship.
Did he use the keyboard to teach you improvising? I’ve always been curious as to how people teach improvising, if they don’t provide some kind of harmonic set-up.

Well you know we would work on improvising but he didn’t teach me per se. He gave me the tools for learning how to do it, but he used to play the chords, he used to plunk out the chords on the piano and I’d blow some choruses on various standard tunes, things like that. But learning how to improvise, that’s something — you really learn how to do it on your own. Nobody teaches you how to do it. They just sort of create the settings for you to experiment in. I think Joe approached it that way. And he gave me the tools for trying to hear and reach the things that I wanted to be able to play.
